title: Arsenal’s ticket craze: Crystal Palace’s ‘enhanced measures’, £1.2k for Burnley game?
content:
Arsenal fans’ desire to watch their team potentially secure a first Premier League title in more than 20 years has seen their final-day opponents Crystal Palace implement “enhanced security measures” for ticketing of the fixture, while tickets for their next game at home against Burnley on Monday are being listed on resale websites for more than £1,200 for one seat.

If Manchester City fail to beat Crystal Palace on Wednesday, Mikel Arteta’s side could lift the Premier League title — for the first time since 2004 — as soon as Monday if they beat already relegated Burnley at the Emirates Stadium, in what will be their final home match of the campaign.

More than 2,500 tickets on the ticket search engine SeatPick — which shows the range of prices listed on resale sites — has many seats for the Burnley game listed as being available for well into four figures for executive-level seats, while a single seat ranges from £650 to £1,200.

The most expensive adult season ticket at Arsenal for the 2025-26 season, excluding hospitality, is £2,112, covering 23 matches (this includes four Champions League ties), while the cheapest is £1,127.

Due to the strict resale policy enforced by the club and the Premier League, there are no guarantees that ticket holders who purchased through a secondary resale website will even be permitted entry into the Emirates.

Palace, meanwhile, said on Tuesday that they have disabled ticket sharing for the final-day fixture at Selhurst Park, and “any supporter found sharing a ticket will be banned from buying a season ticket or membership next season”. The south London club, who face Rayo Vallecano in the Conference League final three days after the game, added that tickets will only be available to those who had a club account before December 1, and that “enhanced security checks” with searches will be in place on matchday.

Several of the ticket platforms listing tickets are categorised as “known unauthorised ticket websites” by the Premier League. SeatPick also appears on this list.

Under UK law, the practice of buying and selling unauthorised Premier League tickets is illegal.

However, multiple secondary-ticket resale websites are registered overseas, which means those platforms operate outside of the UK’s jurisdiction and remain available to UK-based buyers.

SeatPick, for example, is a marketplace that effectively acts a ticket search engine and comparison website and is headquartered in Israel.

In some cases, the tickets listed on some sites for Arsenal’s match against Burnley do not specify seats and instead highlight an area — ‘Shortside Upper Level’, for example.

The cheapest resale tickets are listed for £400, although they are in the away section, and some are still being listed for upwards of £1,200.

Arsenal operate one of the strictest approaches to ticket resales, and the club actively monitors unauthorised websites for illegal resale of tickets and also conducts ID checks on matchdays.

To further prevent resales, they only recognise their own ticket exchange as an authorised marketplace for buying and selling match tickets.

This platform enables the club’s season ticket holders to resell their seats for sold-out home matches to other Arsenal members.

The tickets listed on Arsenal’s marketplace can only be sold at face value, although the seller does not receive the full sale amount as the club charges a 10 per cent admin fee.

For Arsenal’s match against Burnley, tickets on the club’s exchange platform are sold out and can only be purchased by paid-up members of the club’s loyalty programme, which is defined by different membership tiers.

Burnley, who are already relegated, did not sell out their allocation and so offered to return 1,500 tickets to Arsenal. They were then put on Arsenal’s official exchange last week and were sold to members, with priority given to those who missed out in the ballot for tickets originally.

Tickets for Arsenal’s final home game come at a time when demand is arguably at its highest, especially with the club also playing in the Champions League final against Paris Saint-Germain in Budapest on May 31.

There had been some backlash over the number of tickets Arsenal were provided by UEFA, the competition organisers, for the final.

Both finalists were allocated 17,200 (the stadium has a capacity of over 60,000), although Arsenal announced that 16,834 would be made available for general admission.

These were put into a ballot system, and the supporters who were successful were able to begin purchasing their tickets on Wednesday.
